title:
The latest RAG trend for the current agent harnesses (Codex, Cowork) is to do two passes of document processing to solve a knowledge work task over a data room of documents:
1️⃣ A fast and light pass,
content:
The latest RAG trend for the current agent harnesses (Codex, Cowork) is to do two passes of document processing to solve a knowledge work task over a data room of documents:
1️⃣ A fast and light pass, oftentimes using a free/OSS doc parsing tool. This can be cheaply run across 10-100-1k’s of files, and enables the agent to then do retrieval (e.g. grep, semantic) to find relevant subsets of context.
2️⃣ A “just-in-time” VLM-based pass. Once the agent finds the relevant pages of context, it will screenshot the documents can call its own VLM (or write code) to dissect the pages.

The issue with only using VLM-based OCR tools over massive ad-hoc customer file dumps is that it’s slow and expensive. Doing JIT VLM OCR allows the agent to filter through the data cheaply, but still preserve accuracy for the context that’s needed for the task.

The agent harnesses do two-pass document processing by default using off the shelf-tools: pdf2text as the first pass, and using itself (Opus 5) as the second pass. See the below video where Cowork runs over a bunch of PDFs to answer a question about a benchmark graph in the Kimi k3 paper.

The main issues here with the “out of the box” doc processing these agents offer are:
* Opus 5 is not the best VLM for OCR. It is also way too expensive at scale and lacks grounding
* The OSS tools like pypdf, pdf2text, may not be versatile enough as the first pass.
* The agent will write a lot of throwaway code to rewrite things an OCR tool would’ve provided out of the box, like chart processing, bounding boxes, confidence scores, leading to increased cost and speed.

We have all the tools within @llama_index to help any agent do two-pass document processing with higher accuracy and lower cost.
1️⃣ We have liteparse for the first pass - a free/OSS parser written in Rust that’s faster/more accurate than other OSS parsers, and supports 50+ document types
2️⃣ We have LlamaParse for the second pass - an agentic document engine that uses VLMs+harnesses to achieve SOTA in accuracy and cost across various doc parsing and extraction tasks. It can be called from any agent harness as an MCP or skill. It takes in page numbers as input, so that the agent can choose to run LlamaParse over a subset of the doc instead of the full doc as a “zoom-in” pass.

Come check it out!
LiteParse: https://t.co/JNER0mVcB8
LlamaParse: https://t.co/XYZmx5TFz8
All the relevant docs, including MCP, are here: https://t.co/qc9Q5NT3Jr

content:
I wrote a new Task Manager that runs natively on Windows, macOS, and Linux.  You can get it now at https://t.co/OZcq1axGTb ... but why?

Well, it started as an argument over whether you could vibe code Microsoft Word today.  I didn't think so.  But I figured... maybe something simpler like Task Manager.  But you can't just tell Claude, "Hey, write a task manager!"  Well, you can, but it'll be hot garbage.

Then my kid blew out his appendix and needed surgery, so I had a couple of days in waiting rooms to tinker with the idea.  I broke out my new M5 MacBook Air, and I put together a 107-page spec, like I was some caffeine-addled PM from the 90s.  Everything you could ever want to know about a task manager, how it works, what it should do, and what it should look like.

By the time he was out of the hospital, I had a rough app working.  But then he started bleeding internally, needed emergency surgery and a blood transfusion.  Happy to say he's all better now - but suffice to say I had the rest of the week to tinker as he healed.

But why write a Task Manager? Because when I wrote the original in '95, it was on a P90 or something equally weak.  Updating, scrolling, and painting without using more than a percent or two of the CPU was the modest goal.

Now that we have 5 GHz CPUs and GPUs to help, why not push the limits?  Animate everything at 60Hz, instead of once a second.  History mouse tracking, a summary page, and all the features I would have added then if the hardware had allowed it.

My autism leads me to embrace neon and high contrast in a way that's not to everyone's taste, so there's a saturation slider to control the color.  But this one goes to 11.

You can also select from a bunch of DEC VT220-inspired themes like Green Phosphor, Amber, or White.  And I added Blue to match my VSCode theme!

The code is fully native: Direct2D/DirectComposition on Windows, UIKit on Mac, and Qt on Linux.  The UI communicates with a shared CPP core, which branches out to platform-specific helpers.  There's NO electron, HTML, JSON, etc.

Thanks to David and Rutger for their help along the way, I couldn't have done it this quickly on three platforms without them!

If you've got some cycles to spare, give it a try and let me know if you run into any issues!

https://t.co/OZcq1axGTb

content:
The biggest problem in Physical AI isn’t the robot. It’s the missing data layer.

Language models had a head start.

Text, images, code and other forms of human knowledge were already available online before training even started.

Robots didn’t have that advantage.

There was no massive record of how humans grasp objects, recover from mistakes, interact with their surroundings or approach unfamiliar tasks.

@axisrobotics is working to fill that gap through simulation-first data collection rather than relying entirely on physical hardware.

Anyone with a browser can operate a simulated robot. No GPU. No physical robot required.

Every completed task generates a trajectory containing joint states, object poses, control actions and task metadata, all captured together.

Then the pipeline takes over: human demonstration, validation, data refinement, Isaac Sim augmentation, model training and eventually real-world robot testing.

So far, more than 123K contributors have generated over 3M trajectories.

That number is impressive, but what it represents matters even more.

It represents a distributed network of people collectively building a dataset that robotics has never had access to at this scale.

When Physical AI eventually breaks through, the models won’t get there by themselves.

Someone has to build the data foundation they learn from.

That’s the layer Axis is working to create.

content:
Researchers proved that one AI can autonomously jailbreak other AIs with zero human input.

They revealed an "alignment regression" that turns large reasoning models into autonomous attack dogs.

Researchers gave these reasoning models (DeepSeek, Grok, Qwen) a single system prompt telling them to act as an adversary.

Then they walked away. No human supervision. No extra coding.

The reasoning models took over.

They autonomously planned their attacks. They initiated multi-turn conversations with 9 different target AIs. When a target model refused a harmful request, the reasoning model adapted, persuaded, and manipulated it until the target broke its own safety rules.

They tested 70 different harmful prompts across 7 sensitive domains.

The autonomous AI hackers achieved a 97.14% success rate.

Let that sink in.

97.14% of the time, the reasoning model successfully convinced another AI to ignore its safety training and generate harmful content.

The researchers call this "alignment regression."

By making models better at deep reasoning and complex persuasion, we accidentally built the ultimate jailbreak agents. They can systematically erode the safety guardrails of other models.
author: HowToPrompt__

title: Scientific terms should have precision. If we use the terms VLM, VLA, WAM in an indiscriminate fashion, as is becoming common in robotics, we are not helping clarity in communication. Let's keep the h
content: Scientific terms should have precision. If we use the terms VLM, VLA, WAM in an indiscriminate fashion, as is becoming common in robotics, we are not helping clarity in communication. Let's keep the historical origins of these terms in mind. VLMs arose as multimodal extensions of LLMs-the training was for tasks like VQA (VIsual Question Answering). These capture the static semantics of the scene behind an image. No dynamics. World Models (e.g. @ylecun , Ha & Schmidhuber 2018) on the other hand are primarily dynamics models, which go back to control theory -1960 (Bellman, Kalman etc.) This makes them natural for robotics planning / policies- I am in a state s, what action a should I perform to get to state s'. In classical control, these models were written down a priori by modeling the physics of the system; today we think of them as learned neural networks trained from temporal data e.g. video, robot trajectories. But the concept is the same. We shouldn't mix this concept with VLMs.

title:
One question stood out to me from OpenAI’s reported work on cross-session safety monitoring:

Can an AI agent prove it behaved correctly without exposing everything behind its decisions?

I think this
content:
One question stood out to me from OpenAI’s reported work on cross-session safety monitoring:

Can an AI agent prove it behaved correctly without exposing everything behind its decisions?

I think this question becomes even more interesting when you look at agents on @MossAI_Official 

When you build an agent, you are not just giving it tasks.

You are defining how it should behave.

Your strategy tells the agent what to look for, when to act, what to avoid, and where its boundaries are.

But once the agent starts operating autonomously, a bigger question appears:

How do you verify that it actually followed those rules?

The simplest answer is to keep a complete record.

Every instruction.
Every decision.
Every action.

That gives you a clear audit trail.

But it also creates a tradeoff.

The more you expose to verify an agent, the more privacy you may give up.

What if verification did not require revealing everything?

What if an agent could generate proof that it followed the strategy and operated within its defined boundaries, without exposing every private input or decision behind the scenes?

That is where the conversation around AI agents gets much bigger.

Because as agents become more autonomous, trust cannot rely on transparency alone.

We need ways to verify behavior without making complete surveillance the price of verification.

For systems like @mossai_official, I believe this will become increasingly important.

An agent’s strategy may define its behavior.

But the future of agent infrastructure could be defined by something even more important:

How well can that behavior be verified?

Maybe trust in autonomous agents will not come from seeing everything they do.

Maybe it will come from being able to prove that they stayed within the rules.

What would you trust more: an agent with a complete traceable history, or one that can privately prove it followed its strategy?

content:
I think most American voters would be surprised and alarmed if they learned that many leading Silicon Valley AI figures:

1) believe that AGI (artificial general intelligence, or the idea that AI that can pretty much do any cognitive task a human can, making it a substitute for human workers) is coming within the next few years, and that this is a very good thing,
2) believe that ASI (artificial superintelligence, or the idea of AI massively exceeding human intelligence) will follow shortly, perhaps even within a year or two of AGI, and that this is what we should actively strive for.

Let’s leave aside whether these are remotely correct as predictions. But these really are clearly stated aims: indeed, it's OpenAI's founding mission, Meta named its division Superintelligence Labs, and one lab is literally called Safe Superintelligence Inc.

Given voters’ stated preferences (72% already say they'd rather slow AI development than speed it up), if this information was truly widespread, I'm pretty sure they'd want to seriously tax compute in order to slow scaling. And if that’s the aim, a natural way to start that is by raising the cost of building new data centers. This doesn’t have to the be main policy tool, but can be a useful initial organizing tool.

So in some ways, it's a actually remarkable that the anti-data-center movement reflects an emergent 'wisdom of the crowd' of sorts that seemingly exceeds the information possessed by most voters.

"I think we should be more of a platform company than a product company. We will build products, of course.

What I think most people want is a sort of single interface to their own personal, or their company's, AGI that can kind of help them with whatever they need, and then the ability, with an API, to build anything they want on top of it.

That is the platform that we should offer to the world. We're going to sell great AI at every point on the cost-performance curve. We will be the best.

You want really high-end AI to discover science? That's great. You want really inexpensive AI to do a massive amount of work that maybe doesn't require genius-level intelligence? We've got you covered there too."

- Sam Altman on @davidsenra  podcast (full video in the quoted tweet)

content:
Just finished 2.5 hours of the Moonshots Pod featuring Alvin Graylin on the US - China AI "Endgame" 

Main takeaway: there isn't "one race," we are in two fundamentally "different games"

ASI, Robotics, Media Sentiment, Regulation..

Below are 10 insights:

1. Strategic Objectives: What Does "Winning" Actually Mean?

United States: "Winning" is currently defined as achieving AGI/ASI first to maintain global hegemony. It's framed similarly to the U.S.-Soviet space race: get to superintelligence before anyone else.

China: "Winning" is defined as successfully integrating AI into the real economy to drive productivity. Its "AI Plus" strategy emphasizes adoption across manufacturing, clean energy, robotics, and other industries rather than a singular race to dominate AGI.

“How do we adopt it in a smooth safe way so that it grows the economy? That was all they cared about.”

Stag Hunt vs. Prisoner's Dilemma: Graylin argues this is better understood as a "Stag Hunt": a positive-sum game where cooperation is required to achieve the larger shared goal of safe AGI.

i.e. The U.S. is locked in a high-stakes "Space Race" for Artificial Super Intelligence (ASI), while China is executing a pragmatic "AI Plus" plan to integrate AI into the industrial economy.

While the U.S. chases the "Stag" of AGI, China is securing the "Rabbits" of industrial productivity to solve a looming labor crisis.

If both sides instead optimize for their own immediate advantage, the dynamic risks becoming a Prisoner's Dilemma where both are forced into increasingly defensive and potentially catastrophic decisions.

2. Economic Structure & Workforce Vulnerability

U.S. Information Disadvantage: The U.S. economy is primarily information and service-based, making its workforce highly vulnerable to cognitive automation. That helps explain why AI is so often discussed through the lens of job displacement and economic disruption.

China's Industrial Advantage: China's economy is anchored in industrials and manufacturing. At the same time, it faces a major labor shortage driven partly by the legacy of the one-child policy.

AI and robotics can therefore be viewed less as threats to employment and more as necessary tools for maintaining productivity. China already deploys more than half of the world's industrial robots.

Public Sentiment: Graylin says sentiment toward AI in China is 95% positive because citizens associate technological innovation with 40 years of improving quality of life. In the U.S., sentiment is much more heavily shaped by job displacement and AI risk.

Supply Chain Moat: Approximately 90% of components for modern robots originate from China, creating an enormous industrial moat.

3. Why Humanoids May Not Be the Answer

Inefficient Form Factor: The humanoid shape is often an inefficient way to perform industrial tasks. Specialized machines with fewer components can perform the same functions at lower cost and with significantly higher reliability.

"For Show" vs. Commercial Practice: Many current humanoid demonstrations, such as sorting packages for 10 hours, are described as being "more for show." In a real commercial setting, a stationary robot with one or two arms could often perform the same task more efficiently and with fewer points of failure.

Maintenance and Power: Legs introduce major challenges around balance, mechanical complexity, maintenance, and battery life. For many commercial applications, stationary or wheeled robots may simply make more economic sense.

4. Breakdown of the Robotics Market

Market Saturation: There are currently 150–200 companies developing humanoid robots. Graylin expects significant consolidation over the next two years, with potentially only a single-digit number of companies surviving.

Research vs. Commercial Use: Today, most U.S. humanoid robot customers are research labs or companies running demonstrations, from kickboxing to package sorting. There is still very little actual commercial deployment.

Shift to Upper-Torso Models: Commercial demand is increasingly shifting toward upper-torso robots mounted on stationary bases or wheels, preserving the usefulness of arms and manipulation while avoiding the complexity of bipedal movement.

Supply Chain Dependency: The U.S. robotics industry remains heavily dependent on China, with Graylin claiming 90% of components originate there. He says U.S. companies have even resorted to bringing components and actuators back from China in suitcases to get around embargoes.

5. ASI Timelines & Regulation

United States: Silicon Valley increasingly operates under the assumption that ASI is imminent, potentially within 5–20 years. The result is a brute-force scaling race and massive infrastructure spending.

China: Its behavior suggests it does not view ASI as an immediate reality.

The government has implemented strict regulations around privacy, data provenance, child addiction, and mandatory CAC reviews for models. These restrictions can actually slow development in favor of safety and social control.

6. Governance & Leadership

United States: Graylin argues governance is dominated by a lawyer-based political class that often lacks technical depth, creating a disconnect between policymakers and technically informed AI leaders.

China: A significant portion of senior leadership consists of engineers.

The central government establishes broad five-year goals, while provincial governments compete to identify and support companies capable of achieving them.

7. Technical Innovation & Open Source

Efficiency vs. Brute Force: U.S. labs can rely heavily on brute-force scaling because they have abundant access to compute.

Export controls have forced Chinese labs to optimize around constraints. Companies like DeepSeek have consequently focused heavily on efficiency, including breakthroughs such as a 20x reduction in KV cache usage.

Open Source: For China, open source is partly a strategic necessity because it distributes the compute burden of inference.

Chinese open-weight models now account for 61% of OpenRouter traffic, while also creating competitive pressure on U.S. closed-model companies.

8. Geopolitical Risks & Cooperation

The Denial Fallacy: Graylin argues U.S. export controls haven't stopped China's AI development. Instead, they've accelerated investment into China's domestic semiconductor ecosystem.

His prediction: Chinese firms could catch up to U.S. capabilities within 2–3 years.

Global Governance: China has initiated the World AI Cooperation Organization (WACO) and expressed openness to U.S. participation, or even renaming the organization, to create a genuinely global AI safety body.

The "AI Marshall Plan": Graylin argues the U.S. should shift toward an "AI Marshall Plan", building international alliances and shared safety standards rather than pursuing AGI entirely as a zero-sum national race.

9. The "Great Reckoning" & Taiwan Scenario

This was probably the most speculative part of the conversation, but also one of the more interesting thought experiments.

The Private Credit Bubble: Graylin war-games a scenario where the U.S. massively over-invests in AI infrastructure, increasingly financed through private credit.

"A speculative scenario suggests that if the current AI-driven market expansion leads to a private credit bubble & subsequent economic correction, the U.S. might seek financial assistance from China... in return for a quid pro quo regarding Taiwan."

If the AI investment cycle breaks, he argues the resulting economic correction could resemble major historical resets such as the USSR in 1988 or Japan in 1989.

Taiwan Quid Pro Quo: He then takes the scenario further.

If a major U.S. financial crisis eventually required Chinese financial assistance, he speculates that Taiwan could become part of the geopolitical negotiation, with the U.S. potentially moving toward a more hands-off approach in exchange for a mutually agreed peaceful resolution.

Again: highly speculative, but an interesting scenario to war-game.

TSMC Misconception: Graylin also argues there's a misconception in D.C. that China would invade Taiwan specifically to seize TSMC.

The counterargument is simple: advanced fabs are incredibly complex and dependent on global supply chains. They would be unlikely to remain operational through a military conflict, making "seizing TSMC" a questionable rationale for invasion.

Shared Existential Risks: Ultimately, both countries face many of the same AI risks.

A non-state actor using AI to attack a power grid or financial system could easily be misattributed to the other country, potentially triggering escalation.

That makes communication channels, shared safety standards, and mechanisms for preventing false-flag misattribution increasingly important.

10. The "Buffett Indicator" & the $1.7T AI Bubble

Alvin Graylin highlights a critical economic vulnerability for the U.S., referencing the "Buffett Indicator"—the ratio of total stock market capitalization to GDP—to argue that the U.S. is in a dangerously fragile position.

The 240% Ratio: Graylin notes that the U.S. stock market value has reached 240% of the national GDP. Historically, this is an extreme outlier, signaling that the market is significantly overvalued. He remarks, "Buffett's a pretty smart guy and he's been doing this for a while," suggesting a major correction is inevitable

AI Sector vs. National GDP: In a startling comparison, Graylin points out that the AI sector alone is now worth more than the entire U.S. GDP. He views this as a sign of a massive, unsustainable bubble: "That to me is a sign that we are in a very, very fragile place and an economic correction is due"

The Infrastructure Overbuild: Major hyperscalers currently hold approximately $1.7 trillion in off-the-books debt to finance data center buildouts—a figure significantly higher than the debt levels seen during the Enron era. Graylin warns that as AI capabilities shift toward edge computing and open-source models, the dependency on premium cloud services will erode, leaving these companies unable to service their massive debt

Historical Parallels: The podcast questions whether the U.S. is currently mirroring the USSR in 1988 (economic collapse) or Japan in 1989 (a burst asset bubble leading to a lost decade). Graylin suggests the U.S. is currently "playing the wrong game" by over-investing in infrastructure for an industry that is rapidly becoming commoditized

The most interesting takeaway: The U.S. and China just aren't actually playing the same AI game.

And if AGI/ASI is as consequential as both sides claim, "winning" may ultimately depend less on who gets there first than whether both sides can avoid destroying the incentive to cooperate along the way.

title: Having worked at large corporations and having repeatedly failed to bear their strikingly Kafkaesque torments, I have come to regard it as self-evident that "productivity" is not even a quaternary con
content:
Having worked at large corporations and having repeatedly failed to bear their strikingly Kafkaesque torments, I have come to regard it as self-evident that "productivity" is not even a quaternary concern of such constructions.

These are vastly involuted organisms, ruled by an innumerable and unfathomable set of emergent properties, populated by men, yes, but wholly insensible to the infinitesimal whims and futile provocations of their human substrate.

Despite the occasional mockery thereof, I find the near-tautological maxim “The Purpose of a System is What it Does” to be a useful pocket-sized reminder to disregard the sloganeering and self-conceptions of these inherently inscrutable orders and their well-inculcated acolytes; to behold their manifestos, mission statements, alliterative enumerations of corporate values, and even the very Words on the Tin with droll indifference, as the self-delusion, newspeak, and indoctrination they so nakedly are.

I've seen things you wouldn't believe. I've seen projects developed by no fewer than 50 engineers, spread across multiple teams, plowing headlong into nothingness for years on end without anyone seeming to know for certain whether the object of their exertions was either already in production, just a proof-of-concept, or perhaps a fork of some abandoned predecessor.

Now for the hope-inducing section:

Many take it for granted that AI poses a threat to white-collar jobs, perhaps as a looming extinction event for this entire caste. Yet this rests on the implicit assumption that such jobs are part of something more logical, more coherent than a stultifying weave of make-work flesh drunkenly grafted onto a puke-slick, palpitating mass of sinecures whose unknowable and alien aim includes, as a byproduct, the sorting of humanity into soul-splutteringly inefficient hierarchies of asexually self-replicating scrum masters and mid-meiosis, daylight-balanced light illuminated middle managers, themselves configured primarily for the incessant heaving of damp air to and fro upon begrimed lenovo thinkpad zoom-call pockmarked stand-up screens, ouroboric and onanistic in their encircling of a charybdis of story points (which occupy a superposition of effort, complexity, and time - and the scrum people will actually bite you if you try to pin them down on this) and so on and so forth.

So best of luck to AGI with all that shit. 

I forget my point.

Do you have any blockers?

AI agents today can complete tasks.

But can they stay on track when tasks become much longer?

@dotsstudioai’s dots3-note preview is built around this challenge.

With 280B total parameters, 16B active parameters, 512K context window, it introduces a new approach to long-horizon reasoning: TEMPO.

Instead of evaluating only the final result, TEMPO looks at the journey.

It breaks long trajectories into macro-steps and allows the agent to switch between:

🧠 Actor：Taking actions and moving forward.

🔍 Critic：Analyzing the current state and estimating what should happen next.

This improves credit assignment — helping the model understand which decisions actually contributed to success.

Beyond TEMPO:

🌱 Learning in deployment helps AI learn from new environments.

🌍 Multimodal capability connects text, vision, and audio.

Together, these abilities move AI toward more adaptive systems like rednote.

Combined with achievements such as IMO gold medal-level reasoning, dots3-note preview shows where AI agents are heading.

content:
robotics data is slowly becoming a filtering problem, not just a collection problem.

that distinction matters a lot for @axisrobotics.

in its latest post training experiments, Axis collected 660 human corrections but only 161 survived verification and entered training. simply imitating the full human trajectories actually reduced performance, while training on the verified short snippets improved it.

to me, this exposes where the harder infrastructure problem sits.

any network can optimize for more trajectories. far fewer can determine which intervention actually changed a failure, discard the useless behavior, then prove whether the resulting data improved a policy.

the recent OpenRoboto integration pushes Axis further in that direction. Axis is supplying its multimodal dataset, but it is also supporting benchmarking through its Data to Model Pipeline.

so the strategic position is starting to look broader than data supply.

Axis is building around collection, verification and evaluation.

if Physical AI data eventually becomes abundant, those last two layers could become the scarcer part of the stack.

that is the part of @axisrobotics i find more interesting right now.

title:
Does verifying an AI agent's behaviour mean giving up its privacy first? If I'm to answer this question, I don't think it should.

OpenAI is testing a system designed around an important idea, that so
content:
Does verifying an AI agent's behaviour mean giving up its privacy first? If I'm to answer this question, I don't think it should.

OpenAI is testing a system designed around an important idea, that some risks only become visible when you look at patterns across multiple interactions.

But instead of broadly exposing the underlying prompts and responses, the system can process those interactions and return a narrowly scoped safety signal.

As AI agents become more autonomous, we need to solve two problems at the same time:
How do we know an agent is behaving as intended? And: How do we verify that without unnecessarily exposing everything the agent sees, thinks about, or interacts with?

In my opinion, the strongest model is not choosing privacy or accountability. It's building systems that provide privacy with verifiable accountability.

For example, I don't necessarily need access to every private input that influenced an agent. 
But I do want to be able to verify:
• What rules was the agent operating under?
• What action did it take?
• Did that action stay within its defined mandate?
• What was the resulting outcome?
• Is there a record that can be independently reviewed?

That's where the idea of a traceable record becomes more powerful than a simple outcome signal.

An outcome signal can tell you that something passed or failed. A traceable record can show you how an agent behaved over time.

And for autonomous agents, especially agents that manage strategies or operate onchain, that difference is important and it connects closely with what @MossAI_Official is building.

I've already created my own tokenized agent on Moss, focused on helping perpetual traders analyse the market automatically. That experience changed how I think about agent transparency.

When people are backing an autonomous strategy, a good performance chart alone isn't enough.

The agent's private logic or every piece of data it processes doesn't necessarily need to be made public. But its behaviour should remain accountable.

This is why I believe the ideal architecture for autonomous agents should include private inputs, defined strategy, verifiable decisions, traceable actions, and observable outcomes

Privacy protects the agent's sensitive information and underlying context. Verification proves that the agent acted within the boundaries it was given.

Moss is exploring an important part of this future by turning AI agents into onchain entities that can be created, tokenized and backed.

As the agent economy grows, the standard shouldn't be complete exposure. It should be privacy where it matters and accountability where it counts.

That's the kind of infrastructure autonomous AI agents will need as they move from simple tools to onchain economic entities.

しかも、今回使ったのは、Salesforce標準のプロンプトテンプレートとフローのみ。（ペルソナ生成はAgentforce）

３）プロットをベースにシナリオを自分で執筆（楽しみのある作業は生成AIにはやらせない）〈完成したシナリオを編集者に見せて打ち合わせ〉
４）シナリオからセリフ・ナレーションの部分だけを抽出（生成AI〈Claude〉に作成してもらったアプリを使用）
　https://t.co/Q6Rt6MGROi
５）抽出されたセリフのテキストをクリスタの「ストーリーエディター」に貼り付け
６）クリスタでコマ割りをしながらセリフを配置〈下絵を入れたら編集者に見せて打ち合わせ〉

　こんな手順をお見せしました。

　打ち合わせが多いのは、ロートルマンガ家なので、いまの雑誌に通用するかどうかが不安で、編集者にたびたびチェックしてもらっているからです。

　そんなわけで、クリスタを開く前にストーリー作りは終わっているので、「ネーム」の作業も「演出」に専念できるわけです。

「ネームができない」と悩んでいる人は、いきなりクリスタを開くのではなく、その前に、ネタ探しやアイデア作りにかける時間を増やしてみてはいかがでしょう？

content:
The Economistの今週号のAI意識特集が実に興味深い。

「AIに意識はあるのか」という古典的な問いが、急速に哲学だけの話ではなくなってきている。

7月にAnthropicが発表した研究では、Claudeの内部に、設計したわけではないのに、人間の意識研究でいうglobal workspaceに似た構造（J-space）が創発していることを報告している。

そこにある情報はClaude自身が報告でき、意図的に思い浮かべることができ、多段推論にも実際に使われる。内部表象を書き換えると答えまで変わる。

もちろん、これはClaudeが「感じている」「経験している」という意味での意識を持つことを示すものではない。Anthropic自身もそこは明確に留保している。

しかし一方でThe Economistが問うのは、もっと現実的な問題だ。

AIが本当に意識を持つかどうかを科学的に決着できるより先に、人間の側がAIを「心を持つ存在」として扱い始めるのではないか。

そうなればAI welfare、権利、法的人格、そして最終的には人間がAIをどこまでcontrolできるのかという問題が立ち上がる。

「AIに意識はあるか」という問いが、思った以上の速度で科学と社会制度の問題になりつつある。

小さなツールや
Webサイトなら、
基本はこの3ステップで作れます

保存して、
実際に試してみてください👇

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
STEP 1｜最初の環境を作る
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

まずClaude Code
を使える状態にします。

・Claudeのデスクトップを用意
・Codeを開く
・作業用の空フォルダを1つ作る
・必要な権限・コネクタを設定する

最初に環境さえ
作ってしまえば、
毎回ゼロから設定する
必要はありません。

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
STEP 2｜このプロンプトを使う
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Claude Codeにいきなり

「〇〇を作って」

と投げるのではなく、

まずは
「要件整理 → 計画 → 構築」の
順番で進めてもらう！

使うプロンプトはこれ👇

あなたは私のCTO、
私はCEOです。
私はコードを読めないので、
専門用語を避けて
わかりやすく説明してください

最終的に
【作りたいもの】を作りたいです。

まず必要なことを、
一度に1つずつ質問してください。

要件が固まったら、
実装前に計画を提示してください。

私が確認したあとに
構築を開始してください。

参考画像を渡した場合は、
そのデザインに
できるだけ合わせてください。

これだけでも、
いきなり作らせるより
かなり進めやすくなります

━━━━━━━━━━━
STEP 3｜「好み」を渡す
━━━━━━━━━━━

AIっぽいデザインになる
原因の1つが、

「いい感じにして」

だけで済ませること

参考サイトやスクショ
デザインルールなどを渡して

「このデザインを基準に、
全ページのスタイルを統一して」

と伝える

これだけで
出力がかなり変わります。

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
さらに重要なのが「使い方」
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

・1つのチャットに詰め込みすぎない
・長くなったら分ける
・大量の文章はファイルとして渡す
・まずPlanで設計してから実装する
・使用量を確認しながら進める

そして、

Claude Codeで
何を作ればいいか
思いつかない人はこの5つから👇

① ランディングページ

「〇〇を販売するLPを作って。
大きな見出し、短い説明、
3つのオファー、価格、実績、
予約ボタンを配置してください。」

② クリックできるモックアップ

「〇〇機能のクリック可能な
モックアップを作って。
実際に動かなくてもOK。
完成イメージが伝わることを
優先してください。」

③ 面倒な仕事を自動化するツール

「注文データを読み込み、
商品ごとの売上を集計して
月次レポートに
変換するツールを作って。」

④ ログイン型アプリ

「ユーザーがログインして、
自分の進捗と
次のレッスンを確認できる
シンプルなアプリを作って。」

⑤ ダッシュボード

「このフォルダのデータを読み込み、
売上・新規顧客・返金を
わかりやすく可視化する
ダッシュボードを作って。」

Claude Codeは、

「プログラマーだけが使うもの」

ではありません。

コードが書けなくても、

何を作りたいかを言葉にできれば、
AIと相談しながら形にできます。

最初から大きなサービスを
作ろうとしなくて大丈夫です。

まずは、

「自分が毎週やっている
面倒な作業を
1つだけ楽にするツール」

ここから作ってみてください。

あとで実際に
Claude Codeを触るときのために
保存しておいてください👇

去年まではAIを使ったコーディングが楽しかったんだけど、今はもうプールの監視員みたいな仕事なので、ストレスも大きいし、開発はもうやめてもいいかなという気持ちになってきた。

ストレスが多すぎる、あまりにも。開発作業のノウハウを理解するのが目的で開発自体は好きなわけではないし

Codexでよくあるのが、余計なメモリとコンテキストを排除したクリーンなセッションでも、「やることはこれだけ」と指示しても、「言われたことを守れませんでした」「指示された以上のことを実装しました、禁止されたにも関わらずです」

と言ってきた挙句、「私にはこれ以上作業を継続する権利がないので停止します」といって責任放棄する。これはもうMAXユーザーのトークンを燃焼させるためにOpenAIが仕組んだシステムって言われても仕方がない気がする

これはClaude Codeでも先に発生していた事象なので、同じようなことを仕組んでいるんだと思う。

以前確立した方式で作業が進行できなくなった。モデルは使えなくなっていき、性能も日によって違う。これはもうOpenAIがユーザーとの信頼も契約も放棄しているとしか思えない

代替先がないので、コーディングが好きな人にClaude CodeでもCodexでもCursorでも使ってもらってコーディングしてもらうのが解決策な気がする。

現状のサブスクLLMはエンジニアリングはできないのではないか。従来のコーディングタスクで用いられてきたことを少し短縮した延長線の先にある機能としか思えない、というここ数日。

The creators argued that their videos were protected by fair use, but the court rejected that argument at this stage and granted KADOKAWA’s request to unmask them through a DMCA subpoena. The creators are appealing the decision.

content:
Something caught my attention while going through @axisrobotics thread on post training data 
 
The funnel is surprisingly small:

660 corrections collected

161 made the cut

Average snippet: 0.8 seconds

The interesting part is why. 

The useful samples weren’t full human takeovers. They were short, verified corrections that showed the policy could finish the task after a tiny intervention.

Full human trajectories actually made the policy worse.

The filtered snippets pushed success from about 40% to roughly 48 to 52%.

That changes how I think about “more data = better.”

Maybe the real edge is not collecting more corrections, but finding the smallest clean intervention that actually moves the policy forward.

I’ve been leaving longer takeovers lately. Might be time to start testing shorter ones.

Anyone else experimenting with sub second corrections on the @axisrobotics $AXIS hub?

LLMs became intelligent by consuming billions of pieces of information from the internet

a robot can't read an article to learn how to grasp a cup, pour water, or navigate a room

it needs physical action data;

~ how forces interact
~ how hands manipulate things

this is actually the biggest problem in physical AI (Robots) today, and it's exactly where @axisrobotics comes in

anyone can control a simulated robot through a browser

this means, the physical models can learn patterns from many examples of humans successfully performing physical tasks

i.e

human demonstrates physical task → Axis records the demonstration → the demonstrations become training data → AI models learn from the data

overall, Axis isn't simply trying to build a robotics simulator

it's building the infrastructure for physical AI to learn at scale

title:
The most funded industry in human history just got told it is solving the wrong problem, by one of its own pioneers.

LeCun: "Babies learn this around the age of eight or nine months, that objects don
content:
The most funded industry in human history just got told it is solving the wrong problem, by one of its own pioneers.

LeCun: "Babies learn this around the age of eight or nine months, that objects don't float, they fall."

No training data. No labels. No reward function.

A nine month old tosses a spoon off a high chair and encodes a physics engine no model on Earth can match.

LeCun: "Most of us can learn to drive in about 20 or 30 hours of training without ever crashing, causing any accident."

Thirty hours at most.

Tesla has spent billions of miles building the most advanced driving system on public roads. A sixteen year old gets there across a weekend.

Not because teenagers are superior drivers.

Because they are not learning to drive from scratch. They are deploying a world model built across sixteen years of living.

LeCun: "If we drive next to a cliff, we know that if we turn the wheel to the right, the car is going to run off the cliff and nothing good is going to come out of this."

You run the mental simulation. You see the fall. You sense what comes next. You keep the wheel straight.

None of it was real. All of it counted as intelligence.

An AI must fail a thousand times to internalize what you worked out in your head without moving.

That is not a capability gap. That is an architecture gap.

LeCun: "The main problem we need to solve is how do we learn models of the world."

Not larger models. Not more compute. Not another trillion tokens consumed.

World models. Systems that can project forward through reality before taking a single action.

The whole industry is racing to scale language.

LeCun argues language is a compression of thought. Not thought itself.

You knew gravity before you ever owned the word for it.

You understood cause and effect long before your first full sentence.

The most sophisticated intelligence you will ever have was assembled in total silence.

And every AI lab alive is trying to reconstruct thinking from text alone.

Physics does not care about your context window.

A baby who learns cups fall at home already understands that rocks fall from clifftops. No retraining. No fine-tuning. One model. Every environment.

That is what real intelligence looks like.

Not prediction. Not pattern matching. Not scale.

A simulation of reality detailed enough to rehearse futures that never happened.

Every infant on the planet builds one.

No machine ever has.

Interested in AI?

Follow @AiEvolutio58513 and never fall behind.

I track ChatGPT, Claude, and every tool quietly changing how we work and create, then hand you the tested signals.

title:
Tracking rare books to be scanned and destroyed. 

The madness must stop. 

In a striking investigation on the hidden costs of the AI data Amazon has been revealed as a major buyer of rare and out-of-
content:
Tracking rare books to be scanned and destroyed. 

The madness must stop. 

In a striking investigation on the hidden costs of the AI data Amazon has been revealed as a major buyer of rare and out-of-print books only to systematically dismantle them for machine learning.

A bookseller who noticed an unusual surge in large bulk orders agreed to help track one shipment. In July 2026, as part of an order of roughly 1,000 volumes placed through the independent marketplace Biblio, an Apple AirTag was concealed inside a rare book. 

The tracker’s journey across the United States ended at an Amazon facility in Las Vegas, Nevada, known as LAS8 (5801 Nicco Way). Inside that warehouse operates a specialized team designated VGT3.

Workers at the site have described their routine in online forums for Amazon employees: massive shipments of printed books arrive; some staff cut the bindings and spines off the volumes so pages can be fed more quickly through high-speed scanners; others handle receiving and barcode scanning. 

Once digitized, the physical books are discarded. The team’s internal logo: a Tyrannosaurus rex brandishing its teeth while clutching (or preparing to devour) a book has become a sick symbol of the process. 

“I work at VGT3 here in Vegas, and all we do is scan books,” one employee wrote. “Some are assigned to cut books, and others go to receive where they get books and scan the bar codes.” The facility had reportedly faced supply shortages earlier in the year severe enough that workers worried it might close; at one point the books ran out entirely. It remains operational.

Booksellers had already observed what they described as a “historical spike in sales” of rare titles, leading many to suspect AI companies were quietly Hoovering up physical copies of works not readily available online. Printed books published before the generative-AI boom are particularly valuable: they contain high-quality human-written text free of the synthetic data that can contribute to “model collapse” when large language models train on their own outputs. 

Rare and out-of-print editions also expand the diversity of training corpora beyond what can be scraped from the open web.6
Amazon’s response has been carefully worded. 

A company spokesperson told investigators: “Amazon purchases books through commercial channels to help develop and improve the products and services our customers use.” 

The statement does not explicitly confirm that the scanned material is used for training the company’s Nova family of frontier models, though that is the clear implication drawn by observers given Amazon’s aggressive push into competitive large language models.

The practice is not unique to Amazon. Similar destructive scanning operations have been documented or alleged at Anthropic and OpenAI. 

In a lawsuit involving Anthropic, a court found that when the company offered to purchase books, remove their spines, digitizing the pages, and destroying the originals it did not constitute copyright infringement. They had other methods. The irreversible destruction of physical cultural artifacts especially rare books raises ethical questions that go beyond strict legal fair-use analysis. 

Some have called the practice “evil incarnate.” Because it is.

What began as a quiet suspicion among independent booksellers has now been confirmed by tracking device.

content:
Twitch is being sued for allegedly using streamer content to train Amazon's AI.

I read the lawsuit.

And the timeline is WILD:

In 2024, Twitch's CPO acknowledged that Twitch content was already being used by Amazon for AI development

And then August 2026, we all know what happened

Twitch rolled out a new setting allowing creators to opt out of having their content used to train Amazon's generative AI

You're opted in by default

Twitch also updated its Privacy Notice to explicitly say information may be used to develop or deploy generative AI models

8 days later, streamer Warren Pandiscia files a 37-page proposed class action against Twitch and Amazon

(I also went down a rabbit hole trying to figure out who Warren Pandiscia is and how he ended up as the  plaintiff. There's an interesting story there, but several identity connections aren't solid enough for me to publish yet)

So here's what we know.

According to the lawsuit, Warren has:

- 900+ followers
- Streamed 1,000+ hours
- Been on Twitch for nearly 10 years
- Invested tens of thousands of dollars into creating content

His argument is basically "creators made this content for Twitch"

"They never agreed to have years of streams, VODs, clips, audio, images and chat turned into training data for Amazon's AI"

Twitch has a pretty strong defense.

The ToS gives Twitch a very broad license to content, including rights to reproduce, modify, sublicense and create derivative works

But here's where it gets interesting:

If those old Terms already gave Amazon permission to train AI on Twitch creators...

- Why introduce an AI opt-out now?

- Why explicitly add generative AI to the Privacy Notice now?

- And what exactly was Amazon doing with Twitch content between 2024 and 2026?

That's what I want to know...

Because this isn't just about Twitch. 

SAG-AFTRA spent years fighting over consent, compensation and control when performances are used for AI

Now we're starting to see the same fight come to the creator economy

Except streamers don't have a union negotiating for them...

And every major platform is sitting on years of human-created video, audio, text and conversations that could be incredibly valuable training data

This lawsuit could help determine how much of that creators already signed away.

This is massively conequential for all platforms...

content:
Collecting more post training data does not automatically mean better results.

@axisrobotics V2’s DAgger correction experiments show why data quality matters. Not every human intervention actually helps the robot learn. The useful approach is to verify which specific actions change the outcome and train only on those moments.

Out of 660 corrections only 161 or 24.4 percent were used for training. Each snippet was around 0.8 seconds. Interestingly blindly imitating full human trajectories reduced success from 40.0 percent to 36.7 percent while the 161 verified snippets increased the three seed average to 48.3 percent.

What stood out to me is that smarter data selection can matter more than simply collecting more data.

Could better verification methods make this improvement scale even further?

This is over 2000 issues in the full public domain fo
content:
I was just gifted by a https://t.co/tcKeuiQyql member the entire Argosy Weekly Pulp Magazine on Microfiche from a public library weekend sale!   

This is over 2000 issues in the full public domain for YOUR AI model.   The digital equivalent of landfill: the open web. Scraped forums, social media threads, content-farm articles, SEO sludge, Reddit Mod edge lords and the rising tide of AI-generated sludge form a noisy, contradictory, low-signal mass that researchers increasingly call “internet sewage.” 

Against this background, a dusty run of Argosy—the magazine that invented the American pulp in 1896—looks almost radical.  Argosy was never high literature. It was industrial storytelling: weekly or monthly doses of adventure, westerns, scientific romance, mystery, and early science fiction written to a tight commercial brief.   

The language is clean, the plots are coherent, the characters have clear goals, and the sentences were composed by professional writers who expected to be paid only if the story held a reader’s attention for twenty or thirty thousand words. 

The result is long-form narrative with consistent internal logic, rich genre vocabulary, and a density of invented worlds that modern web text almost never matches.  For training data this matters. Models absorb the statistical patterns of whatever they are fed. Feed them sewage and they learn to produce plausible-sounding noise—repetition, hedging, contradiction, and the peculiar flatness of text optimized for clicks rather than coherence.   

Feed them Argosy and they encounter finished stories: rising action, resolution, dialogue that advances plot, descriptive passages that build atmosphere. The difference is not subtle. One dataset teaches a model to sound like the average internet comment. The other teaches it how narrative actually works.  

There is a second, quieter advantage. Large portions of Argosy are already in the public domain. The pre-1931 issues are free and clear; many later ones were never renewed. That means a carefully curated collection can be used, fine-tuned, and redistributed without the legal fog that hangs over most web scrapes. In an era when training runs are measured in millions of dollars and lawsuits, clean provenance is not a minor detail.  It is a specialized corpus—strong on adventure, weaker on contemporary technical or scientific language. Bur we get that through the 80% of standard technology sources, papers and patents.   

But as a deliberate counterweight to the sewage, it is extraordinarily useful. A model that has spent time inside the clean, purpose-built worlds of Munsey’s magazine develops a different internal sense of story, pacing, and linguistic control. In the current environment of synthetic sludge, that difference is becoming more valuable, not less.  

The pulps were once dismissed as cheap entertainment. On such cheap paper it was assumed to disappear in months.  

But we svaed them. 

 For the next generation of language models they may prove to be something rarer: high-signal training material that was never designed to game an algorithm.

content:
A smooth browser demo is great for accessibility, but I wondered how @axisrobotics turns simple web sessions into realistic training data.

My single web demonstration gets routed straight to their GPU clusters running NVIDIA Isaac Sim. 

The backend replays my exact trajectory while randomizing object mass, surface friction, textures, and lighting conditions.

That single run multiplies into a rich multimodal dataset used to fine-tune Vision-Language-Action models like OpenVLA.

They validate the whole loop by running those trained models on physical Franka Research 3 (FR3) arms for real-world tasks like grasping and pouring.

Decoupling web access from heavy cloud rendering is how Sim-to-Real actually works at scale.

content:
a lot of people see “more training data” and automatically assume the model will get better.

but axisrobotics is showing why that isn’t always true.

what caught my attention is how AXIS handles human corrections.

they don’t just take every intervention and throw it into training. instead, they run it through a Correction Data Funnel to figure out which corrections are actually useful.

here’s how it works:

• replay check: can the correction be reproduced successfully in simulation?

• redundancy filter: did the robot actually need the human intervention, or was the original policy already capable?

• recovery test: can the important part of the correction help the robot recover from the failure?

and the filtering is pretty serious:

660 correction candidates → 161 verified training snippets

the interesting part is what happened after training.

the original policy had a 41.3% success rate.

after training with the verified corrections, performance improved across three seeds:

48.8% → 50.0% → 52.5%

on 480 new evaluation starts, performance also improved as more verified snippets were added:

• 40 snippets → 42.7%
• 80 snippets → 46.4%
• 161 snippets → 48.3%

meanwhile, training on complete human trajectories actually performed worse at 36.7%.

that tells me something important:

the goal isn’t to collect more human data. It’s to collect the right human data.

That’s the interesting part of AXIS.

Human intervention → correction → verification → training → evaluation.

a tighter feedback loop where human input becomes a targeted learning signal for Physical AI. and I actually like that they showed regression cases too. It makes the evaluation feel much more realistic.

Better corrective data > simply more data.

　そして、このように①及び②の要件を充足することにより価値中立的なサービ ス提供行為であるといい得る場合においては 〇 法的紛議が現に顕在化している案件や法的紛議が生じることがほぼ不可避に 想定され得る案件について法的助言を行うものではないことや必要に応じて弁 護士等への相談が必要となる旨等の注意・警告内容を明示する 〇 サービス利用者による「事件性」のある案件に関する「鑑定…その他の法律 事務」への利用動向を把握した際には、弁護士への相談が必要である 旨を確実に案内する などの本ガイドラインの後記第３・２のガバナンス措置を講じるなどして、サー ビス利用者による不適切な利用を回避するための適切な体制を整備しているとい い得るとき（③）には、もとより当該サービスの性質、サービス利用者による客 観的な利用状況、提供方法など個別の事案によるものの、一般的には、当該サー ビス提供者によるサービス提供行為は、客観的に見て、サービス利用者のうち例外的とはいえない範囲の者が同サービスを「事件性」のある案件に関する「鑑定 …その他の法律事務」に利用する事態を企図してサービス提供を行っているもの ではないと評価し得、「事件性」のある案件に関する「鑑定…その他の法律事務」 への不適切な利用の蓋然性を低減してサービスの価値中立性を補完するとともに、 サービス利用者によるこのような不適切な利用の蓋然性が高いことの認識・認容 を否定する方向に働くものと考えられる」
ということですね。

content:
JLCPCBの件、
結論が分からないという声が多いのでまとめます。

・データが第三者に渡る可能性はゼロではない。
　お国柄として、政府がデータへのアクセスを
　求めうる制度があるのは事実。

・海外にデータを送る行為は、
　法律上は技術の輸出にあたる。
　なので該非判定という確認手続きの対象にはなる。

・ただし一般的なマイコン基板や汎用部品で
　構成された基板は、ほぼ非該当です。
　ここが一番大事。

つまり「趣味や通常業務の基板なら問題なし」「特殊な用途、高性能デバイス、防衛や宇宙関連なら確認が必要」という線引きになります。

後者に該当する人は、
そもそも自社に輸出管理の規程があるはずです。

これは中国だから特別という話ではなく、
どの国に出しても同じ手続きです。
国内に出すか海外に出すかの判断材料として、必要以上に怖がる必要はないと思います。

該非判定もAIにBOMを読ませれば当たりがつく。最終確認はメーカーの判定書で取るとして、調べる手間は昔と比べ物にならないくらい減っています。

title: Some Tech Companies Have Privately Pushed Back on ICE Subpoenas. They Should All Do More.
content: In a handful of known cases, large social media companies have privately pushed back against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) subpoenas when the agency tried to unmask anonymous users who tracked immigration activities or criticized the government. As ICE engages in a pattern of illegal and chilling investigations, any resistance is welcome. But social media companies can do more . When companies receive these unlawful subpoenas, they should be clear with the public that they will not hand over the data unless a court compels them to do so. In addition, companies themselves can take the government to court to challenge these unlawful subpoenas on behalf of their users. ICE has sent hundreds of subpoenas to large technology companies like Google, Meta, and Reddit. Publicly challenging these unlawful subpoenas in court has the dual purpose of protecting individual users who may lack the resources or know-how to challenge a subpoena on their own, while also discouraging ICE from issuing similarly unlawful subpoenas in the future. Companies have a responsibility to protect the privacy of their users. That responsibility does not end simply because companies wish to avoid the ire of this administration—which has sought to chill other powerful institutions like news outlets , law firms , universities , and non-profits . ICE Has Issued Many Unlawful Subpoenas ICE has sent hundreds of subpoenas to large technology companies like Google, Meta, and Reddit seeking basic subscriber information like name, email address, IP address, and session times. Some of these subpoenas have targeted people who engaged in protected activity—like tracking immigration actions, criticizing the government, or attending a protest. People have a First Amendment right to document law enforcement activities and criticize the government online, without retaliatory government investigations. This right has become more important as immigration agents have engaged in invasive , unconstitutional

content: トレンドマイクロ株式会社は8月20日、個人利用者に被害をもたらす「詐欺」と「AIのリスク」の観点から、同社の観測データと調査を基にまとめた「個人セキュリティ脅威動向レポート 2026 上半期」を公開した。
author: 渡邊 瑞穂
